chapter.title: Reasoning About the Design and Execution of Research
chapter.scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT Physics, Mathematics and Research Reasoning lessons. Models and calculations use stated assumptions. Independent scientific review is pending; this is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: A scientific hypothesis is a testable explanation; a prediction is an expected observation under specified conditions. Evidence can constrain an explanation without proving it true for all possible cases.
An experiment compares outcomes while controlling relevant conditions. A useful hypothesis makes predictions that could be contradicted by observations.
Failure to reject a hypothesis is not proof of truth. Null results can arise from limited precision, low power or a genuinely small effect.
Replication and revision are normal parts of inquiry. Distinguish an exploratory idea from a prespecified test when evaluating the strength of a claim.

steps.text: An experiment manipulates an independent variable and measures a dependent outcome. A control condition helps separate the tested change from background effects.
A confounder is related to both exposure and outcome and can distort the apparent association. Holding conditions fixed, random assignment and appropriate analysis address different sources of bias.
Random assignment allocates treatment and supports causal comparison within a study. Random sampling selects participants or units from a population and addresses a different generalization question.
Biological replicates are distinct experimental units; repeated readings of one specimen are technical replicates. Treating all technical readings as independent can overstate precision.

steps.text: An interventional study assigns an exposure, whereas an observational study measures exposures without assigning them. Observational associations need careful treatment of confounding.
Random assignment can reduce systematic baseline differences on average but does not guarantee perfect balance in every finite sample. Blinding addresses expectation and measurement biases.
A cohort study follows groups defined by exposure; a case-control study selects on outcome status and compares prior exposures. These sampling choices affect which measures can be estimated directly.
Study design alone does not guarantee validity. Loss to follow-up, adherence, outcome measurement and the population actually studied all affect interpretation.

steps.text: Ethical research requires attention to voluntary informed consent, reasonable risk–benefit balance, privacy and fair participant selection. These are principles for evaluating a study, not a substitute for jurisdiction-specific rules.
Consent is an ongoing process that supports understanding and choice. A signature alone does not establish comprehension or remove the need to respect withdrawal.

steps.text: Internal validity concerns whether a study’s conclusions hold for its studied comparison. External validity concerns applicability to other populations, settings and conditions.
A statistically detectable effect can be too small to matter practically. Consider absolute change, uncertainty, baseline risk and costs rather than relying only on a p-value.
Selective reporting and publication patterns can distort the apparent literature. Prespecified outcomes, transparent methods and replication improve interpretability but do not guarantee correctness.
Translation to practice depends on feasibility, adherence, context and competing evidence. A laboratory mechanism or single trial is one contribution to a broader evidence base.
